lessons.title: Forces and their interactions
lessons.summary: Understand the difference between scalars and vectors, sort forces into contact and non-contact types, calculate weight using W = mg, and find resultant forces using free body and vector diagrams.
objectives: I can explain the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of each.
I can describe the difference between contact and non-contact forces and identify the pair of objects involved in a force.
I can calculate weight using W = mg and explain what is meant by centre of mass.
I can find the resultant of forces acting along the same line and draw a free body diagram.
I can use a scale vector diagram to find a resultant force or resolve a force into two components (Higher).

activities.title: Scalars and vectors
activities.content:
## Scalars and vectors

Every physical quantity is either a **scalar** or a **vector**.

- A **scalar** has **magnitude (size) only**. Examples: mass, speed, distance, time, temperature, energy.
- A **vector** has **magnitude AND direction**. Examples: force, velocity, displacement, acceleration, momentum, weight.

The pairs *distance/displacement* and *speed/velocity* are the classic exam favourites. If you walk 3 m east then 3 m west, your **distance** is 6 m (scalar), but your **displacement** is 0 m because you are back where you started.

### Drawing vectors
A vector is drawn as an **arrow**:
- the **length** of the arrow represents the magnitude,
- the **direction** of the arrow shows the direction.

A force of 20 N to the right and a force of 20 N to the left have the same size but are different vectors because they point in opposite directions. We often use a sign convention, for example right = positive and left = negative, so those two forces would be +20 N and −20 N.

question.text: Which THREE of the following quantities are vectors?
question.hint: A vector needs a direction to describe it fully. Would it make sense to say 'north' after the quantity?
question.explanation: Force, velocity and displacement all have a direction, so they are vectors. Mass, temperature and time are scalars: they have size only.

options.feedback: Mass has no direction: 5 kg north makes no sense.

activities.title: Contact and non-contact forces
activities.content:
## What is a force?

A **force** is a push or a pull that acts on an object because it is interacting with another object. Forces are measured in **newtons (N)**.

There are two families of force:

| Contact forces (objects touching) | Non-contact forces (objects separated) |
|---|---|
| friction | gravitational force |
| air resistance (drag) | electrostatic force |
| tension (in a rope or string) | magnetic force |
| normal contact force (a surface pushing back) | |

### Forces come in pairs
Whenever two objects interact, **both** objects experience a force. The two forces are **equal in size and opposite in direction** and they act on *different* objects. This is Newton's third law, and you will meet it again in the motion sub-topic.

Examples:
- A book resting on a table: the book pushes **down** on the table, and the table pushes **up** on the book with an equal normal contact force.
- Two magnets: the north pole of magnet A pulls on magnet B, and magnet B pulls back on magnet A with the same size of force.
- The Earth pulls you down (your weight); you pull the Earth up with exactly the same force. The Earth's huge mass means it barely moves.

question.text: Match each situation to the type of force that best describes it.
question.hint: Ask yourself: do the two objects have to be touching for the force to act?
question.explanation: A brake pad rubbing on a wheel is friction (contact). A compass needle turning towards north is a magnetic force (non-contact). A skydiver slowed by the air experiences air resistance (contact with air particles). An apple falling from a tree is pulled by gravity (non-contact).

pairs.left: A brake pad rubbing against a bicycle wheel
A compass needle turning to point north
A skydiver slowing as they fall through air
An apple falling from a tree

activities.title: Weight, mass and gravity
activities.content:
## Weight is a force

**Mass** is the amount of matter in an object, measured in **kilograms (kg)**. It is a scalar and it does not change wherever you go.

**Weight** is the **force of gravity** acting on an object, measured in **newtons (N)**. It is a vector that always acts **towards the centre of the planet** you are on.

Weight depends on the mass and on the **gravitational field strength**, $g$:

$$W = m g$$

- $W$ = weight in N
- $m$ = mass in kg
- $g$ = gravitational field strength in N/kg

On Earth $g$ = **9.8 N/kg**. On the Moon it is only about 1.6 N/kg, so a 60 kg astronaut weighs 588 N on Earth but only 96 N on the Moon, even though their mass is still 60 kg.

Weight and mass are **directly proportional**: double the mass and the weight doubles. Weight is measured with a calibrated spring balance called a **newtonmeter**.

### Centre of mass
The weight of an object can be treated as acting at a single point called its **centre of mass**. For a symmetrical object of uniform density this is at the geometric centre. On a free body diagram the weight arrow starts at the centre of mass and points straight down.

activities.title: Worked example: weight on Earth and Mars
activities.content:
**A Mars rover has a mass of 900 kg. Calculate its weight (a) on Earth where g = 9.8 N/kg and (b) on Mars where g = 3.7 N/kg.**

(a) On Earth:
$W = mg = 900 \times 9.8 = 8820$ N

(b) On Mars:
$W = mg = 900 \times 3.7 = 3330$ N

The rover's **mass is 900 kg in both places**. Only the weight changes because the gravitational field strength is different.

**Rearranging the equation.** A crate weighs 490 N on Earth. What is its mass?

$m = \dfrac{W}{g} = \dfrac{490}{9.8} = 50$ kg

Always check the units: kg × N/kg = N, so the kg cancel out and you are left with newtons.

question.text: A student has a mass of 55 kg. Calculate the student's weight on Earth. Use g = 9.8 N/kg.
question.hint: Use W = m g and multiply the mass by the gravitational field strength.

activities.title: Resultant forces and free body diagrams
activities.content:
## Resultant force

When several forces act on one object, we can replace them with a single force that has the same overall effect. This single force is the **resultant force**.

For forces acting along the **same straight line**:
- forces in the **same direction add up**,
- forces in **opposite directions subtract**.

A car engine pushes forward with 3000 N while friction and drag pull back with a total of 2200 N. The resultant force is 3000 − 2200 = **800 N forwards**.

If the resultant force is **zero**, the forces are **balanced**. The object either stays still or keeps moving at a steady velocity. If the resultant is **not zero**, the object **accelerates** in the direction of the resultant force.

## Free body diagrams
A **free body diagram** shows a single object as a simple box or dot with **every force acting on it** drawn as an arrow. Rules:
- draw arrows from the object outwards, in the direction the force acts,
- make the arrow length roughly proportional to the force,
- label each arrow with the force name and size,
- only include forces acting **on** the object, not forces it exerts on other things.

```
        ↑ normal contact force 500 N
   ←  [ BOX ]  →  push 40 N
 friction 40 N
        ↓ weight 500 N
```

Here the vertical forces balance and the horizontal forces balance, so the resultant is zero.

question.text: A boat is pushed forwards by its propeller with a force of 1800 N. Water resistance acts backwards with a force of 1250 N and the wind pushes the boat backwards with a further 150 N. Calculate the resultant force on the boat.
question.hint: Add the two backward forces together first, then subtract from the forward force.
question.explanation: Backward forces = 1250 + 150 = 1400 N. Resultant = 1800 − 1400 = 400 N forwards.

question.text: True or false: if the resultant force on a moving cyclist is zero, the cyclist must be slowing down.
question.hint: What does a zero resultant force do to the motion of an object that is already moving?
question.explanation: False. A zero resultant force means the forces are balanced, so the cyclist carries on at a constant velocity. Slowing down needs a resultant force acting backwards.

activities.title: Vector diagrams and resolving forces (Higher)
activities.content:
## Forces that are not in a straight line (Higher tier)

When two forces act at an angle to each other, you cannot just add or subtract. Instead you draw a **scale vector diagram**:

1. Choose a scale, e.g. 1 cm = 10 N.
2. Draw the first force as an arrow to scale.
3. Draw the second force starting from the **tip** of the first arrow (tip-to-tail).
4. The **resultant** is the arrow from the start of the first force to the tip of the last force.
5. Measure its length and convert back using the scale; measure its angle with a protractor.

For two forces at right angles you can check with Pythagoras: two forces of 30 N and 40 N at 90° give a resultant of $\sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50$ N.

## Resolving a force
The reverse process is called **resolving**: one force at an angle is split into **two components at right angles** (usually horizontal and vertical) that together have the same effect. Draw the force to scale as the diagonal of a rectangle; the sides of the rectangle are the components.

A sledge pulled by a rope at 30° above the ground gets only part of the pull horizontally (the useful part) and part vertically (which slightly lifts the sledge). Resolving lets you work out each part.

An object is in **equilibrium** when the resultant force is zero. On a tip-to-tail vector diagram this means the arrows form a **closed shape** that ends exactly where it started.

question.text: Two tugboats pull a ship. One pulls north with a force of 60 kN and the other pulls east with a force of 80 kN. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force on the ship in kN.
question.hint: The forces are at right angles, so the resultant is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.
question.explanation: Resultant = √(60² + 80²) = √(3600 + 6400) = √10000 = 100 kN, acting at an angle between north and east.

question.text:
A shopping trolley of mass 20 kg is at rest on level ground.

(a) Calculate the weight of the trolley. Use g = 9.8 N/kg. (2 marks)

(b) State the size and direction of the normal contact force from the ground on the trolley. (1 mark)

(c) A shopper now pushes the trolley forwards with a force of 50 N and friction acts with a force of 35 N. Calculate the resultant force and state what happens to the trolley's motion. (2 marks)
question.hint: For (b), the trolley is not moving vertically, so the vertical forces must be balanced.
question.explanation: (a) W = m g = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N. (b) The normal contact force is 196 N acting upwards, balancing the weight. (c) Resultant = 50 − 35 = 15 N forwards, so the trolley accelerates forwards.

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Scalars** have size only (mass, speed, distance). **Vectors** have size and direction (force, velocity, displacement) and are drawn as arrows.
- **Contact forces** need touching (friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force). **Non-contact forces** act at a distance (gravity, magnetic, electrostatic).
- Forces occur in **pairs**: equal in size, opposite in direction, acting on different objects.
- **Weight = mass × gravitational field strength**, $W = mg$, with $g$ = 9.8 N/kg on Earth. Weight acts at the **centre of mass**.
- The **resultant force** replaces all the forces with one. Zero resultant = balanced forces = no change in motion.
- (Higher) Use **scale vector diagrams** drawn tip-to-tail to find resultants, and **resolve** a force into two perpendicular components.

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Speed is a scalar because it has magnitude only. Velocity, weight and acceleration all have a direction.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: the mass of an astronaut is smaller on the Moon than on Earth.
practiceQuestions.hint: Which quantity depends on gravitational field strength: mass or weight?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere. It is the weight that is smaller on the Moon because g is smaller there.

practiceQuestions.text: A bag of cement has a mass of 25 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth. Use g = 9.8 N/kg.
A rock weighs 32 N on the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is 1.6 N/kg. Calculate the mass of the rock.
practiceQuestions.hint: Rearrange W = m g to make m the subject.

metadata.blanksText: When two objects interact, the forces on each object are ___ in size and ___ in direction.

practiceQuestions.explanation: Interaction pairs are equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on the two different objects.

practiceQuestions.text: Three children pull on a rope. Two pull to the left with forces of 120 N and 90 N. One pulls to the right with a force of 250 N. Calculate the size of the resultant force on the rope.
practiceQuestions.hint: Total the forces on each side, then find the difference.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Left = 120 + 90 = 210 N. Right = 250 N. Resultant = 250 − 210 = 40 N to the right.

practiceQuestions.text: A parachutist is falling at a steady speed. Which TWO statements are correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: Steady speed means the forces are balanced.
practiceQuestions.explanation: At steady speed the resultant force is zero, so air resistance equals weight. The weight does not change during the fall; it is the air resistance that has grown until it matches the weight.

options.text: The resultant force on the parachutist is zero
Air resistance is equal in size to the parachutist's weight
The parachutist's weight has decreased to match the air resistance
options.feedback: Weight depends only on mass and g, neither of which has changed.

options.text: Air resistance is larger than the weight

practiceQuestions.text: Put the steps for finding a resultant force using a scale vector diagram in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: You cannot draw anything until you have chosen a scale.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Choose the scale, draw the first vector, add the second tip-to-tail, draw the resultant from start to finish, then measure and convert.
order: Choose a suitable scale, e.g. 1 cm = 5 N
Draw the first force as an arrow to scale
Draw the second force starting from the tip of the first
Draw the resultant from the start of the first arrow to the tip of the second
Measure the length and angle of the resultant and convert using the scale

practiceQuestions.text: Explain the difference between the mass and the weight of an object.
practiceQuestions.hint: One is a scalar measured in kg, the other is a force.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg, and is the same everywhere. Weight is the force of gravity on the object, measured in N, and depends on the gravitational field strength.

markScheme.criterion: Mass is the amount of matter / measured in kg / does not change with location
Weight is the force of gravity / measured in N / depends on gravitational field strength

practiceQuestions.text:
A garden roller is pulled by a handle. The pull of 200 N acts at an angle of 60° above the horizontal.

(a) Describe how you would use a scale drawing to resolve this force into a horizontal component and a vertical component. (2 marks)

(b) Using cos 60° = 0.5 and sin 60° = 0.87, calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the pull. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (b), the horizontal component is F cos θ and the vertical component is F sin θ.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Draw the 200 N force to scale at 60° to a horizontal line, then complete a rectangle with horizontal and vertical sides; the side lengths, converted using the scale, give the components. (b) Horizontal = 200 × 0.5 = 100 N; vertical = 200 × 0.87 = 174 N.

markScheme.criterion: Draw the force to scale at 60° to the horizontal
Complete a rectangle / draw perpendicular lines and measure the horizontal and vertical sides
